Series Editor’s Pref ace
Margot Waddell

Since it was founded in 1920, the
Tavistock Clinic has developed a wide
range of developmental approaches to
mental health which have been strongly
influenced by the ideas of psychoanalysis.
It has also adopted systemic family ther-
apy as a theoretical model and a clinical
approach to family problems. The Clinic
is now the largest training institution in
Britain for mental health, providing post-
graduate and qualifying courses in social
work, psychology, psychiatry, and child,
adolescent, and adult psycho therapy, as
well as in nursing and primary care. It
trains about 1,700 students each year in
over 60 courses.

The Clinic’s philosophy aims at promot-
ing therapeutic methods in mental health.
Its work is based on the clinical expertise
that is also the basis of its consultancy and
research activities. The aim of this Series
is to make available to the reading public
the clinical, theoretical, and research work
Velocita di lettura 5%

that is most influential at the Tavistock
Clinic. The Series sets out new approaches
in the understanding and treatment of
psychological disturbance in children,
adolescents, and adults, both as individ-
uals and in families.

As the editors of Sibling Matters say in
their Introduction, “Sibling relation-
ships can be some of the most intimate,
enduring, troubling, and conflictual re-
lationships that we may experience in
our lives”. This is a powerful and utterly
recognizable statement to any who work
with children, young people, and families
and also, of course, to all who have siblings
themselves. That description stands be-
side the equally powerful evocation, again
in the Introduction, of the plight of Hansel
and Gretel in the mythic fairy-tale. The
survival of these two children in the face
of the witch's wicked intentions is only
by virtue of their sibling cooperation and
life-saving ingenuity. The editors stress
that the children’s “need to make their way
home”, separately across “a great stretch of
water”, is a potent reminder of the neces-
sity, in reality, for each child “to make his
or her own way in life”.

And so the book begins. As it proceeds,
one starts to realize what a comprehensive
and original exploration it is of so many
major facets of sibling life, here accorded
the detailed attention that has been
Velocita di lettura 5%

lacking hitherto, at least where the early
and adolescent years are concerned. Beau-
tifully—I even want to say impeccably—
edited, the successive chapters in the early
part of the book lead the reader across a
range of thoroughly researched theoretical
perspectives that bear on sibling rela-
tionships, from Freud, through Klein and
Anna Freud, to contemporary attachment
and systemic thinking. These chapters in
Parts I and II offer a scholarly, historical,
and contemporary picture of the broaden-
ing and deepening of an understanding of
this unique relationship.

From Part III of the book onwards, the
emphasis is on siblings at different points
in the life cycle: infancy and young child-
hood, followed by middle childhood, then
on to adolescence. Part IV focuses on
siblings in very different contexts: those
of divorce and the “looked after” system,
the latter accompanied by an account of a
significant piece of clinical research into a
psychotherapeutic assessment model for
those in care. The final part of the book
movingly addresses the impact and cross-
generational legacy on siblings of illness
and death.

The editors have succeeded in their
self-appointed task to, as they say in the
Endpiece, bring together theory, research,
and clinical work. They themselves and
their chosen contributors more than fulfil
Velocita di lettura 5%

this task—a difficult one, to say the least.
To marshal and integrate what, from the
outside, look like very disparate ways of
thinking, to bring together the outer and
the inner worlds of these complex rela-
tionships, is a huge achievement. Research
and clinical work are not always easy
bedfellows, but the editors’ commitment
to good practice sings through their own
extensive contributions and those of their
chosen authors with compelling force and
professionalism.

Acknowledgements
Throughout the book, the contributors
give testimony to the significance of
sibling relationships. First of all, we
would like to thank all the siblings, from
early childhood to parenthood, who have
informed and enriched our clinical ex-
perience and played a major role in the
creation of this book. But we are reminded
by Margaret Rustin, who has been a pion-
eer among child psychotherapists in work
on sibling issues, that there are many ways
in which we might encounter this aspect
of our lives in professional training and
work—as “analytic siblings”, as co-work-
ers, and as colleagues. In light of this, we
would like to thank our many co-workers
with whom we have shared cases and our
colleagues with whom, over the years,
we have discussed sibling matters. We
are grateful to all the contributors to the
book, who gave their time and shared their
experience, often juggling this with com-
peting demands.

Special thanks go to Nina Harris for her
helpful advice on chapters 8 and 9 and

to Margaret Rustin for her thoughts on
chapter 2 as well as her agreement to write
the Foreword.

We are grateful to Margot Waddell as
Series Editor for her valued support. We
wish to thank the Karnac production team
for its excellent work. We also thank Trina
Hayes and Pamela Sinclair for precious
help in copy-editing the manuscript.

Finally, and perhaps fittingly, we dedi-
cate this book to our respective siblings,
Barbara and David.

Note on confidentiality

Throughout the book, all names of per-

sons referred to have been changed and

every effort has been made to disguise
their identity, but not in ways that change
the meaning of the clinical material
discussed.

About the Editors

and Contributors

Gill Gorell Barnes has been working with
children and families since the 1960s,
both in the Child and Family Department
at the Tavistock Clinic and at the Institute
of Family Therapy which she co-founded
with colleagues in the 1970s. As Training
Director she subsequently co-founded the
Master’s Degree in Systemic Family Ther-
apy with Birkbeck College, London. The
nature of her work has always reflected
the changing nature of family life, in-
cluding divorce, stepfamily living, single-
parent family living and the growth of gay
and lesbian family life. She has written
three books on working with families in
social change and has co-authored an-
other five, and she has written over fifty
scholarly articles and chapters relating

to working with families. Currently she
continues to teach internationally and is
writing a book about working with fathers
who are attempting parenting in extreme
family situations.

Velocita di lettura 5%

Judy Dunn is Professor of Developmental
Psychology at the Institute of Psych-
iatry in London. Her research interests
include children’s emotional and socio-
communicative development as well as
parent, child, sibling, and peer relation-
ships. Her longitudinal research includes
several studies of children in the US and
the UK, focusing on their relationships
with family members (including siblings
and grandparents). Recent books include
Children’s Views of Their Changing Families
(2001), Children’s Friendships: The Begin-
nings of Intimacy (2004), and Families
Count: Effects on Child and Adolescent De-
velopment (2006).

Ricky Emanuel is a Consultant Child

and Adolescent Psychotherapist, Head

of Child Psychotherapy Services at the
Royal Free Hospital, London, and an
adult psychotherapist. He trained at the
Tavistock Clinic and teaches there as well
as at the Birmingham Trust for Psycho-
analytic Psychotherapy. He also teaches
and lectures abroad. He has published a
number of articles and contributed chap-
ters to several books. Publications include
Anxiety (2000); “On Becoming a Father—
Reflections from Infant Observation” (in
Fathers Today, ed. Trowell et al., 2002); and
“Thalamic Fear” (Journal of Child Psycho-
therapy, 2004).

Debbie Hindle is a Consultant Child and
Adolescent Psychotherapist, trained at
the Tavistock Clinic where she also re-
ceived her Doctorate in Psychoanalytic
Psychotherapy (Child) for her work on
the assessment of siblings in foster care.
She is retired from the NHS, but for the
previous ten years she was Head of the
Clinical Training in Child Psychotherapy
at the Scottish Institute of Human Rela-
tions in Edinburgh and worked clinically
in a specialist Child and Adolescent Mental
Health Service in Glasgow for children
who were fostered or adopted. She has
written extensively, including two co-
edited books: Personality Development: A
Psychoanalytic Perspective (1999) and The
Emotional Experience of Adoption: A Psy-
choanalytic Perspective (2008).

Alexander Kriss is a doctoral candidate
of clinical psychology and is based in New
York City. Since 2008 he has trained at
The New School for Social Research and is
currently completing his internship year
at Columbia University Medical Center.
His research and clinical interests involve
a pluralistic mixture of psychoanalysis,
attachment theory, existentialism, and
the intersection of mental health with
popular culture and public policy. Recent
publications from 2013 include a chap-
ter on psychoanalytic psychotherapy in
Velocita di lettura 6%

Current Psychotherapies (ed. D. Wedding &
R. J. Corsini) co-authored with Jeremy D.
Safran, and a paper in the journal Research
in Psychotherapy exploring the use of nar-
rative interviews to assess attachment and
reflective functioning in adolescents, co-
authored with Howard and Miriam Steele.
Lisa Miller is now retired from the NHS
but was for many years a Consultant Child
Psychotherapist in the Child and Family
Department at the Tavistock Clinic and
formerly Chair of the Department. She ran
the Under Fives Service and chaired the
Under Fives Workshop. One of her leading
interests is infant observation, and she co-
edited the book Closely Observed Infants
(1989) with Margaret Rustin, Michael Rus-
tin, and Judy Shuttleworth. She has taught
and lectured extensively in the UK and
abroad and published in the field. She con-
tinues to teach and supervise.
Inge-Martine Pretorius qualified asa
child and adolescent psychotherapist at
the Anna Freud Centre (AFC). She is the
manager of the Parent-Toddler Service at
the AFC where she runs a weekly parent-
toddler group. She is a Clinical Tutor for
Psychoanalytic Developmental Psych-
ology at University College London and
the Anna Freud Centre where she organ-
izes and teaches the MSc Psychoanalytic
Perspectives on Child Development

Velocita di lettura 6%

course. She works part-time in the NHS,
running a Child Psychotherapy Outreach
Service in a nursery school on a large
housing estate. She has published in the
field of molecular genetics and psychoana-
lysis and is co-editor with Marie Zaphiriou
Woods of Parents and Toddlers in Groups:
A Psychoanalytic Developmental Approach
(2010).

Marguerite Reid is a Consultant Child
and Adolescent Psychotherapist who has
worked in the field of perinatal mental
health for many years. She co-founded

the innovative Perinatal and Infant Men-
tal Health Service based in Chelsea and
Westminster Hospital, London. Her re-
search interest is traumatic delivery and
perinatal loss and the impact this has on
the mother, the parental couple, and the
siblings in the family. She has published a
number of papers in the field of perinatal
health. She recently trained as a couple
psychotherapist at the Tavistock Centre
for Couple Relationships.

Susan Sherwin-White was until recently
a Consultant Child and Adolescent Psycho-
therapist and Child Psychotherapy Lead at
Hammersmith and Fulham CAMHS Child
and Family Consultation Centre in the
West London Mental Health NHS Trust.
She has now retired from the NHS. She
has been Chair of the Association of Child
Velocita di lettura 6%

Psychotherapists. She taught on Freud for
many years at the Tavistock Clinic for the
Observational Studies course. She has a
number of clinical publications on child
and adolescent issues, with a particular
focus on brother-sister psychology. She is
currently engaged in research on Melanie
Klein’s development of work with children
and young people.

Margaret Smallbone was trained at the
Tavistock Clinic. She has had a life-long
interest in young people in public care
and has been keen to find ways to make
analytic psychotherapy work for them.
She is author of Psychotherapy with Young
People in Care: Lost and Found (2001),

and contributed to The Handbook of Child
Psychotherapy (ed. A. Horne & M. Lanyado,
1999/2009) and to Direct Work: Social
Work with Children and Young People in
Care (ed. B. Luckock & M. Lefevre, 2008).
She is a Consultant Child and Adolescent
Psychotherapist in a busy CAMHS team
(Hertfordshire Partnership Foundation
NHS Trust). She continues to consult to
various Looked After Children Services

in England, with a particular interest in
helping residential staff and foster carers
use reflective skills for children in their
care.

Howard Steele is Professor and Director
of Graduate Studies in Psychology at the
Velocita di lettura 6%

New School for Social Research in New
York City. At the New School, he co-directs
(with Miriam Steele) the Center for At-
tachment Research. He is also senior and
founding editor of the international bi-
monthly journal Attachment and Human
Development, and he publishes widely

on the topics of parenting, attachment,
loss, trauma, and emotion understanding
across the lifespan and across generations.
He and Miriam Steele were co-editors of
the 2008 volume, Clinical Applications of
the Adult Interview. He is founding and
current President of the Society for Emo-
tion and Attachment Studies (SEAS).
Miriam Steele is Professor and Director
of the Doctoral Program in Clinical
Psychology at the New School for Social
Research in New York City. At the New
School, she co-directs (with Howard
Steele) the Center for Attachment Re-
search. She is also an Anna Freud Centre-
trained psychoanalyst and a member of
the American Psychoanalytic Association.
She initiated the London Parent-Child
Project, a major longitudinal study of
intergenerational patterns of attachment
that gave rise to the concept of “reflective
functioning”. She has also carried out
longitudinal research in the contexts of
child maltreatment and adoption. Most
recently, together with H. Steele and
Velocita di lettura 6%

Anne Murphy, she has pioneered the de-
velopment of a Group Attachment-Based
Intervention aimed at preventing child
maltreatment and promoting attachment
security.

Foreword

Margaret Rustin

This ambitious book, edited by two very
experienced child psychotherapists, who
also share a commitment to high stand-
ards of scholarship, brings together think-
ing about siblinghood from a number

of perspectives and some distinguished
writers. Strongly represented in Part [

are the contributions of psychoanalytic
theory—Sigmund Freud, Melanie Klein,
and Anna Freud are each accorded an im-
pressively meticulous chapter exploring
their observations and understanding of
the place of siblings in the construction
of our mental universe and of the vicissi-
tudes of relationships influenced by our
identity as siblings across the lifespan.
There has been an expanded interest

in this dimension of our internal world
within British psychoanalysis in recent
years (Coles, 2003, 2006; Lewin & Sharp,
2009; Mitchell, 2000, 2003), and child
psychotherapists have noted that their
own clinical framework has given more
Velocita di lettura 6%

space to these preoccupations over many
decades, as the chapters on Klein and
Anna Freud prefigure. The essence of this
thinking is conveyed in a wonderful short
paper by Martha Harris, “Brothers and
Sisters” (1967a).

Part II represents the editors’ conviction
concerning the importance of integrating
psychoanalytic and other theoretical para-
digms. They draw on empirical psycho-
logical research on family relationships
(the peerless Judy Dunn, whose book with
Carol Kendrick on siblings presented such
wonderful accounts of sibling lives; Dunn
& Kendrick, 1982a), attachment research,
and systemic family therapy theory and
practice. These chapters are major sum-
maries of large bodies of work and are
rewarding to read. Their inclusion here
makes a real contribution to the editors’
aim of expanding dialogue between adja-
cent intellectual traditions.

The subsequent sections take us to
what child psychotherapists bring to this
field. We start with babies, babies who
become big brothers and sisters, and new
babies entering a world in which someone
else has already occupied mother’s lap.
Lisa Miller’s characteristically energetic
prose and deep sympathies for parents
and young children remind us strongly
of the way that clinical intuition is best
grounded in the very detailed observation
Velocita di lettura 6%

on which child psychotherapy training
places such a high premium. The editors
take the story forward into middle child-
hood and adolescence, and these chapters
include some fascinating clinical cases

of work with twins—an exceptional kind
of sibling experience. As there seem to be
increasing numbers of twins around in
the context of assisted reproduction, this
focus is most timely.

The final two parts are rooted in clinical
practice, one focusing on varieties of fam-
ily contexts (divorce, reconstituted fam-
ilies, step-siblings, etc.) and on the lives
of children in care, and the second on the
effects of illness and death of a sibling. The
chapters that explore psychotherapeutic
work with children in the care system
—such a core element in the caseload of
most contemporary child psychotherap-
ists—bring to life the intensity and long-
lastingness of sibling feeling in children
who have lost their first family home.
Research recently undertaken by Liselotte
Grunbaum (unpublished doctoral thesis,
2014) in Denmark adds to that reported
by Debbie Hindle in very striking ways:
neither of these researchers expected to
find quite the degree of emotional inten-
sity between siblings that their research
revealed. It may well be that the kind of
clinical evidence that child psychotherapy
can uncover and interrogate has a vital
Velocita di lettura 7%

part to play in taking seriously sibling
matters in the lives of very young children
whose experience is less open to other
forms of investigation.

The very painful final chapters on sibling
loss and illness, including one that de-
scribes the effects of early loss in the next
generation, are written by outstanding
specialist practitioners working in hos-
pital contexts. The tragedies to which such
children have been exposed in either the
recent or more distant past are matched
by the skill and devotion of their ther-
apists, leaving the reader with hope that
these children’s pain can be mitigated and
their life-energies freed for the future. The
specialist units that Ricky Emanuel and
Marguerite Reid have championed could
not have more elegant testimony to their
importance.

This is a big book, and I hope it will
inspire more writing about sibling rela-
tionships arising from clinical experience.
Some of the themes that remain to be
explored that occur to me are these: the
meaning of being a singleton; the “feel” of
big and small families; group work with
siblings; the differences between being
or having a brother and being or having a
sister, and between families of children of
both genders and families of only one; and
the way that cousins can be both virtual
siblings but also provide another whole
Velocita di lettura 7%

family world. From my own clinical and
life experience, I am impressed by the
frequent loneliness of the only child and,
in my work with adult patients, by the
persisting importance of sibling loves and
hates. In a clinically based book such as
this, it is inevitable that difficulties loom
large and that sibling friendship, com-
panionship, and devotion are less to the
fore. The recently published book Young
Child Observation (Adamo & Rustin, 2013)
provides some material on observation of
ordinary young children’s play that may
contribute to this larger picture.

But as so often, literature can expand
and enliven our imagination and under-
standing: think of Shakespeare's sibling or
quasi-sibling characters, who display the
whole range of love, playfulness, loyalty,
possessiveness, rivalry, envy, and hatred—
the twins of Twelfth Night, the quarrelling
brother and sister of Measure for Measure,
the cousins and illegitimate brother of
Much Ado About Nothing, Rosalind and
Celia in As You Like It. The classics in chil-
dren’s literature similarly bear witness
to how siblings are at the heart of things,
from Russell Hoban’s delightfully clear-
minded Frances with her little sister
Gloria, to C. S. Lewis’s quartet exploring
Narnia, J. K. Rowling's vast cast in which
siblings play such a large part (but in
which Harry is so notably alone in his sub-
Velocita di lettura 7%

stitute families)—and, to be inclusive, one
should at least mention Enid Blyton’s Fam-
ous Five.

Meanwhile, this book is a really major
achievement, and we owe a great debt to
the editors’ ambition to join up diverse
strands: Melanie Klein and Anna Freud,
developmental and attachment research,
systemic and psychoanalytic therapy,
clinical theory and clinical practice. It will
undoubtedly be a widely useful source as
well as representing some of the best of
child psychotherapy in the UK.

Sibling Matters
1 minuto rimasto per il cap... 7%

Introduction
When thinking about the complex
nature of sibling relationships, “Am I
my brother’s keeper?” (Genesis 4: 9) is
the rhetorical question that comes to
mind. The fatal blow Cain inflicted on
his brother Abel was the consequence
of jealousy and envy, but the question
implies both that he is not responsible
for his brother and that it is inherently
understood and expected that he should
be. Separateness—the need to be an
individual and the fact that we are inex-
tricably bound to our brothers or sisters
—is at the centre of the tension in sibling
relationships.

In a brief paper, Perlman (1967, p.
148) traces the origin of the term. In her
researches, she found that the word “sib-
ling” is a derivative of the Anglo-Saxon
and then middle-English word “sibb”,
which as a noun meant “related, akin, the
offspring of the same parents”; as an adjec-
tive it meant “intimate, inclined towards,
congenial”. This highlights the intimacy
and complexity of the sibling relationship,
3 minuti rimasti per il capitolo 7%

which is given, not chosen—a relationship
that binds us to the reality of parental pro-
creativity and throws us headlong into the
rough and tumble of life.

In Hansel and Gretel, the children found
themselves threatened with abandon-
ment by their parents and had to pitch
their wits against the power of the witch.
The implication in the story is that the
children would not have survived on their
own and that being together provided
special protection. Neither age nor gender
was a barrier to the children’s ingenuity
in this situation (Hansel’s use of a stick
disguised as a finger, Gretel’s enticement
of the witch into the oven). Towards the
end of the story, as the children make their
way home, they have to cross “a great
stretch of water”. With the help of a little
duck they manage, but only by crossing,
“one after the other” (Brothers Grimm,
1948, p. 93). Bettelheim (1976, p. 165)
says that Hansel and Gretel is “one of many
fairy tales where two siblings co-operate
in rescuing each other and succeed be-
cause of their combined efforts”. Yet their
need to make their way home, across the
water, separately, is a powerful reminder
that in reality each child needs to make his
or her own way in life.

The changing face
of family life
There have been significant changes in
family structures in recent decades in
Western societies, which also raise ques-
tions over who is counted as a sibling. The
weakening of the nuclear family has been
notable with increasing rates of divorce,
separation, and repartnering (or not)
and civil marriages as current features
of family life in the twenty-first century.
The diversity of family composition has
extended the range of who is regarded
as a sibling now when households may
contain full siblings, half-siblings, step-
siblings, and—in the case of removed chil-
dren—foster siblings, adoptive siblings,
and co-residential quasi-siblings (see Ed-
wards, Hadfield, Lucey, & Mauther, 2006).
The complicated dynamics and potential
benefits of this are among the themes ex-
plored in this book.

Over the last sixty years, in the West
and particularly in the UK and US, there
has been a decrease in the size of families
and the number of children per family.
Alongside this, an increasingly ageing
population living longer in the West, and,
2 minuti rimasti per il capitolo 7%

atleast in the UK, the adverse ratio of the
young-people population, is posing (and
will continue to pose) questions over its
care; the role of “siblings” here and the
extended family in looking after elderly
parents (cf. Rustin, 2007) are increasingly
important as state welfare and subsidies
are repeatedly cut back. Economic
pressures will also continue to impact on
parents in their planning for one-, two-,
or more baby families, depending on soci-
ocultural and religious context, and this
again affects the number of siblings avail-
able when adult to care for ageing parents.
Nowhere in the world have these
problems been more starkly illustrated
perhaps than in China, where the 1979
one-child policy, introduced to check huge
population growth (as it successfully did),
has left in its tracks serious social issues,
among which is the care of elderly parents,
regarded as a duty in Chinese custom
(Henley, 2012). The personal emotional
impact of the ban on siblings and experi-
ence of loneliness is poignantly summed
up by the Chinese artist Li Tianbing:
“My generation is unique in China and
the world. We were the first not to know
the meaning of the word ‘brother’ and
‘sister’” (quoted in Henley, 2012).

“Who is a sister and
a brother?”
The question posed by the Family and
Social Capital ESRC Research Group (Ed-
wards, Hadfield, Lucey, & Mauther, 2005)
—“who is a sister and a brother?”—cap-
tures something of the ambiguity and
diversity noted in the above section on
the changing face of family life. From a
biological perspective, a sister or brother
by definition share the same parentage,
and half-siblings one parent. Yet the
many ways of being a family and the
dislocation of children that might be in-
volved presents a more complex picture.
In addition, different ethnic and cultural
groups and societies may have different
definitions of who is a sibling. “This raises
the issue of the importance of culture,
language, interpretation and subjectivity
to constructing definitions, and social and
emotional experiences, of who is a sibling,
rather than a self-evident, biological or
legal state” (Edwards et al., 2005).

Trying to define or categorize sibling
relations has led to the development of
a number of typologies. For example,
Treffers, Goedhart, Waltz, and Kouldijs
2 minuti rimasti per il capitolo 7%

(1990) identified 26 types or possibilities
of sibling relationships. In the field of
social work, Elgar and Head (1999) de-
scribed nine types of sibling relationships
based on genetic relatedness, common
history, family values, and legal status. In
one of the few studies that interviewed
children directly, Kosonen (1999) came to
distinguish between what she called “kin”
siblings, who were known to the children
as being a sibling, and “core” siblings,

who shared the children’s home and with
whom they had emotional ties whether or
not they were biological siblings. In their
qualitative study, in which 58 children
aged 7 to 13 years were interviewed, Ed-
wards et al. (2005) noted that most of the
children made a clear distinction between
family and friends, but more importantly
their descriptions emphasized the import-
ance of the quality of their relationships,
their emotional engagement with each
other (either positive or negative), and a
deep sense of connectedness—of knowing
and being known.

Different perspectives,

shared interests

Sibling relationships can be some of the

2 minuti rimasti per il capitolo 8%

most intimate, enduring, troubling, and
conflictual relationships that we may
experience in our lives. One of the first
publications to draw attention to the com-
plex and profound nature of sibling rela-
tionships was by Bank and Kahn (1941).
Drawing on research and clinical work,
they described and illustrated many im-
portant dynamics in sibling relationships
as well as implications for individual and
family therapy. It was not until the 1980s
that more systematic research was under-
taken in the field of child developmental
psychology about the nature, interactions,
and qualities of sibling relationships, led
notably by Judy Dunn and colleagues. Her
innovative and ground-breaking work
opened the door to further research and
drew attention to and sparked interest in

acquired to offer children psychoanalytic

research were integrated in all aspects of
work. Kennedy (1978) emphasized that
the historical background of the work in
the War Nurseries, “influenced the Clinic’s
choice of later research projects and [the]
continued interest in developmental
studies” (Kennedy, 1978, p. 7). Anna Freud
and her colleagues’ interest in siblings and

Conclusion

It is not surprising that Anna Freud
thought and wrote about siblings
throughout the evolution of her theory of
child development. Her awareness of the
infant’s dependence on maternal care and
of the infant’s immature psyche forced her
to consider the child’s experience of par-
ents and siblings, as well as their influence
on the child. She considered the mother to
play a pivotal role in facilitating the child’s
progress “from greedy stomach-love to

a truly constant love attachment” with
the father and siblings (A. Freud, 1953, p.
16), by helping to bind the aggression and
negativity to create the capacity for am-
bivalence and complex relationships.

Conclusion

Much of the literature on siblings in
adolescence points to this developmental
stage as being a turning point in sibling re-
lationships, as young people increasingly
spend more time with peers and activities
outside the home. Yet this does not convey
the complexity of the findings from de-
velopmental research, which indicate that
siblings remain an important resource of
affection, companionship, and intimacy
(Buhrmester, 1992). The experience of
relations with siblings also shapes young
people’s trust, expectations, and engage-

on substance abuse, older siblings can cast
a powerful influence on younger siblings’
life-style choice in relation to drugs and
alcohol. But they can also be looked up to,
be someone to seek to emulate, challenge,
or even overtake.

The developmental changes and
challenges of adolescence are highlighted
by the process of separation and indi-
viduation, often considered primarily
in relation to parents. But this process is
also played out in relation to siblings. As
poignantly described in several of the clin-

child”, can draw young people into be-

family relationships at a time when their
concerns should be elsewhere. But sibling
solidarity can also provide a protective
factor, both in such adverse situations and
in more ordinary disputes with parents.

In the conclusion to his chapter on “Mov-

possibly the making of the adult life to
come” (p. 197). Similarly, in our opinion,
the sibling dimension, its impact on devel-

This research grew out of clinical work

For some time, I had been struck by the

often posed by referring professionals was

Reviewing the social work literature in

Retrospective studies involving adults

Jones and Niblett (1985) succinctly
summarize the way in which “The argu-

Cumulative trauma

In this study, all the children seen had
been exposed to extreme situations over
extended periods to time. The majority

of these children had suffered profound
neglect and had witnessed violence in the
home—for some, this was combined with
physical or sexual abuse. Not surprisingly,
the themes identified in this study had
many parallels with the consequences of
severe deprivation and abuse so poign-
antly described in Boston and Szur (1983)

and Hunter (2001). To this descriptive
account, the more recent neurobiological

potentially devastating, long-term effects
of childhood trauma on the developing

and cognitive functioning of children
(Balbernie, 2001; Emanuel, 1996, 2004;
Glaser, 2000; Perry, Pollard, Blakley,
Barker, & Vigilante, 1995).

Dunn and Plomin (1990) raised two
issues that have particular relevance to
thinking about siblings in foster care.
First, “stressful events can have a cumula-
tive, cascading effect and the experience
of a series of such events may well make
an individual increasingly vulnerable and
likely to suffer greater negative impact
from future events” (p. 141). Second,
even if siblings have an apparently shared
environment, experience may “impinge
differently on different siblings because of
differences in personality, age or expect-
ations” (p. 158). Taken together, Dunn and
Plomin point to the need to consider the
cumulative impact of events on children
and to the need to differentiate the impact
on each child.

Three themes related to cumulative
trauma emerged in the material and were
also highlighted in the CBCL and Narra-

re- enactment. All point to the pervasive

had lost not only her birth mother but also
a relationship with her natural sibling,
although she enjoyed a warm relationship
with the brothers and sisters that were
part of her adopted family.

This information felt like the missing
piece of the jigsaw in my work with Ms
Gregg. As we thought about the shadow
that had hung over her adoptive mother
and over Ms Gregg’s childhood, her love
for baby Holly grew. At the end of our
work, it was noticeable that she looked
less angry and more feminine, as though
our work had allowed another part of
herself to emerge as she began to embrace
motherhood.

Within this vignette, it has not been pos-

but there was a couple fit of loss and aban-

I quoted Emanuel Lewis and Sandy
Bourne (1989) at the beginning of this

chapter. They stressed that following
perinatal death there were immediate
problems for the mother, but that it is
often in the next generation that difficul-
ties occur. The women described in this
chapter were mothered by a woman who
had experienced a perinatal loss and, as
a result, grew up in the shadow of a dead
infant. Mothers who have experienced a
perinatal loss often speak of feeling that
there is a black hole or gap in the family,
where the lost baby should be. Theres,
perhaps, a fear that any member of the
family may fall through this hole.

I find that women often have a rich
phantasy life associated with the dead
sibling. This can be associated with how
their sibling would have looked, his or her
personality, and the type of relationship
they might have enjoyed. This is perhaps
even more the case when the woman is
then the only child in her family of origin.
She may feel that she has lost a potential
life-enriching relationship with her dead
sibling.

I have mentioned earlier in this chapter
difficulties with rivalry when the sibling
is not present in the family. Children
born following a perinatal loss may well
be scapegoated in their family or may
experience themselves as the “cuckoo in
the nest”. The parental couple and other
siblings in the family have often built up

hopes and expectations about the baby
who has died. The next child may well
experience feelings of survivor guilt, often
leading to suicidal ideation, or of triumph
that they are part of their family while
their dead sibling is not. This can lead to
risk-taking behaviour.

There can often be confusion about
gender if the dead infant was a different
sex. Women can then be left struggling
with issues about their sense of a feminine
identity, unsure whether the lost child
was the gender that the parental couple
would have desired. This can contribute
further to difficulties when the woman
wishes to become a mother.

Lewis and Bourne (1989), as has been
seen, stressed that following perinatal
loss it is often in the next generation that
difficulties occur. The next generation of
women are those some of whom I have de-
scribed in this chapter. They do not have
a strong sense of self, and the importance
of their lost sibling has been an important
factor in their lives. They have benefitted
from psychotherapy during the perinatal
period when they have struggled with
depression, anxiety, and a fear that they
will not be good-enough mothers. The
work has enabled them to develop a sense
of hopefulness about their capacity to
mother, as well as about improving their
own quality of life.

Endpiece

Time and again, the previous chapters
have emphasized the complex and en-
riching nature of sibling relationships.

It is perhaps not surprising that the last
chapter explores the transgenerational
influence of family relationships and the
emotional sequelae of loss on same-gener-
ation siblings and the subsequent impact
on the next generation. Family life—our
most intimate relations and interactions
—shapes our sense of self.

In this book, we have endeavoured to
bring together theory, research, and
clinical work. It is our view that these
different perspectives and the interface
between them provide a fuller under-
standing of sibling relationships. That is,
it seems increasingly necessary to draw
on different sources of knowledge, as well
as understanding the different ways this
knowledge is gathered and analysed. As
we have seen, much can be gained from
observation that records children’s inter-
actions with each other, but also much can
be learned from psychoanalytic infant and

young child observation, where the ob-
server’s emotions are also engaged in the
process and something of the child’s inner
world can be imaginatively understood.
The difference between general findings
and what is specific to an individual high-
lights the tension between research and
clinical work. But we feel, increasingly,
that these different perspectives should
inform good practice. We hope that this
book may provide a useful starting point
for further research and attention to this
issue in clinical work.
